question_text: Your organization's marketing team wants to send biweekly scheduled emails to customers that are expected to spend above a variable threshold. This is the first ML use case for the marketing team, and you have been tasked with the implementation. After setting up a new Google Cloud project, you use Vertex AI Workbench to develop model training and batch inference with an XGBoost model on the transactional data stored in Cloud Storage. You want to automate the end-to-end pipeline that will securely provide the predictions to the marketing team, while minimizing cost and code maintenance. What should you do?

options.text: Create a scheduled pipeline on Vertex AI Pipelines that accesses the data from Cloud Storage, uses Vertex AI to perform training and batch prediction, and outputs a file in a Cloud Storage bucket that contains a list of all customer emails and expected spending.

Create a scheduled pipeline on Cloud Composer that accesses the data from Cloud Storage, copies the data to BigQuery, uses BigQuery ML to perform training and batch prediction, and outputs a table in BigQuery with customer emails and expected spending.

Create a scheduled notebook on Vertex AI Workbench that accesses the data from Cloud Storage, performs training and batch prediction on the managed notebook instance, and outputs a file in a Cloud Storage bucket that contains a list of all customer emails and expected spending.

Create a scheduled pipeline on Cloud Composer that accesses the data from Cloud Storage, uses Vertex AI to perform training and batch prediction, and sends an email to the marketing team's Gmail group email with an attachment that contains an encrypted list of all customer emails and expected spending.

explanation: A is correct because Vertex AI Pipelines and Cloud Storage are cost-effective and secure solutions. The solution requires the least number of code interactions because the marketing team can update the pipeline and schedule parameters from the Google Cloud console. B is not correct because Cloud Composer is not a cost-efficient solution for one pipeline because its environment is always active. In addition, using BigQuery is not the most cost-effective solution. C is not correct because the marketing team would have to enter the Vertex AI Workbench instance to update a pipeline parameter, which does not minimize code interactions. D is not correct because Cloud Composer is not a cost-efficient solution for one pipeline because its environment is always active. Also, using email to send personally identifiable information (PII) is not a recommended approach.

question_text: You have developed a very large network in TensorFlow Keras that is expected to train for multiple days. You want to update the code to run distributed training using tf.distribute.Strategy and configure a corresponding machine instance in Compute Engine to minimize training time. What should you do?

options.text: Select an instance with an attached GPU, and gradually scale up the machine type until the optimal execution time is reached. Add MirroredStrategy to the code, and create the model in the strategy's scope with batch size dependent on the number of replicas.

Create an instance group with one instance with attached GPU, and gradually scale up the machine type until the optimal execution time is reached. Add TF_CONFIG and MultiWorkerMirroredStrategy to the code, create the model in the strategy's scope, and set up data autosharding.

Create a TPU virtual machine, and gradually scale up the machine type until the optimal execution time is reached. Add TPU initialization at the start of the program, define a distributed TPUStrategy, and create the model in the strategy's scope with batch size and training steps dependent on the number of TPUs.

Create a TPU node, and gradually scale up the machine type until the optimal execution time is reached. Add TPU initialization at the start of the program, define a distributed TPUStrategy, and create the model in the strategy's scope with batch size and training steps dependent on the number of TPUs.

explanation: B is correct because GPUs are the correct hardware for deep learning training with high-precision training, and distributing training with multiple instances will allow maximum flexibility in fine-tuning the accelerator selection to minimize execution time. Note that one worker could still be the best setting if the overhead of synchronizing the gradients across machines is too high, in which case this approach will be equivalent to MirroredStrategy. A is not correct because it is suboptimal in minimizing execution time for model training. MirroredStrategy only supports multiple GPUs on one instance, which may not be as performant as running on multiple instances. C and D are not correct because TPUs are not recommended for workloads that require high-precision arithmetic, and are recommended for models that train for weeks or months. Also, TPU nodes are not recommended unless required by the application.

Use key-based hashes to tokenize the features containing PII data, and train the model from scratch.
Use deterministic encryption to tokenize the features containing PII data, and tune the model from the last checkpoint.

B is not correct because masking does not enforce referential integrity, and a drop in model performance may happen. Also, tuning the existing model is not recommended because the model training on the original dataset may have memorized sensitive information. D is not correct because deterministic encryption is reversible, and anonymization requires irreversibility. Also, tuning the existing model is not recommended because the model training on the original dataset may have memorized sensitive information.

question_text: Your BigQuery ML time-series forecasting model needs to predict sales for multiple stores simultaneously. Each store has different sales patterns and seasonality. How should you structure your ARIMA_PLUS model?

options.text: Use a single ARIMA_PLUS model with the TIME_SERIES_ID_COL option set to the store identifier, which trains separate time series models for each store.
Train separate ARIMA_PLUS models for each store and manage them individually in different BigQuery datasets.
Include store as a categorical feature in a single ARIMA_PLUS model to capture store-specific patterns.
Aggregate sales across all stores and train a single ARIMA_PLUS model, then distribute forecasts proportionally to each store.

explanation: A is correct because TIME_SERIES_ID_COL enables training multiple time series within a single model, automatically handling each store's unique patterns while simplifying model management and prediction. B is not correct because managing multiple separate models is operationally complex, harder to maintain, and doesn't scale well as the number of stores increases. C is not correct because ARIMA_PLUS doesn't support categorical features in the way traditional regression models do; it requires TIME_SERIES_ID_COL for multiple series. D is not correct because aggregating sales loses store-specific patterns and seasonality, resulting in poor predictions when disaggregated back to individual stores.

question_text: A streaming media company wants to build a recommendation system that suggests movies to users based on their viewing history and ratings. The company has a large dataset of user-movie interactions stored in BigQuery. Which BigQuery ML model type should you use?

options.text: Create a matrix factorization model using model_type='MATRIX_FACTORIZATION' to learn latent factors for users and movies.

Create a k-means clustering model using model_type='KMEANS' to group similar movies together.
Create a linear regression model using model_type='LINEAR_REG' to predict movie ratings.

B is not correct because while classification could predict if a user likes a movie, it doesn't provide ranked recommendations like matrix factorization does. C is not correct because k-means groups movies but doesn't personalize recommendations based on individual user preferences. D is not correct because while linear regression can predict ratings, matrix factorization is more effective for recommendation systems as it handles sparse user-item interaction matrices better.

question_text: Your retail analytics team needs to forecast daily sales for the next 90 days based on 3 years of historical sales data with seasonal patterns. options.text: Create a time-series model using model_type='ARIMA_PLUS' which handles seasonality and external covariates like promotions and weather.
Create a linear regression model using model_type='LINEAR_REG' with date features as predictors.
Create a boosted tree regression model using model_type='BOOSTED_TREE_REGRESSOR' with engineered time features.
Create a deep neural network using model_type='DNN_REGRESSOR' to capture complex temporal patterns.

C is not correct because while boosted trees can work with engineered features, they don't inherently model time-series patterns and seasonality like ARIMA_PLUS does. options.text: Create an autoencoder model using model_type='AUTOENCODER' which learns normal patterns and identifies transactions that deviate significantly.
Create a logistic regression model using model_type='LOGISTIC_REG' to classify transactions as normal or anomalous.
Create a k-means clustering model using model_type='KMEANS' and treat small clusters as anomalies.
Create a linear regression model using model_type='LINEAR_REG' to predict transaction amounts and flag large residuals.

explanation: A is correct because autoencoders are specifically designed for unsupervised anomaly detection, learning to reconstruct normal patterns and identifying anomalies based on reconstruction error without requiring labeled data. B is not correct because logistic regression requires labeled training data (normal vs anomalous), which is typically not available for anomaly detection scenarios. C is not correct because while k-means can identify outliers, it's less effective than autoencoders for high-dimensional anomaly detection and doesn't provide a clear anomaly score. D is not correct because linear regression is supervised and requires defining what to predict, whereas anomaly detection is typically unsupervised and autoencoders are better suited for this task.

question_text: Your company needs to categorize customer support tickets into one of five priority levels (P0 to P4) based on ticket text and metadata. You have 100,000 labeled historical tickets stored in BigQuery. Which model type should you choose?

options.text: Create a multiclass logistic regression model using model_type='LOGISTIC_REG' which supports classification into multiple categories.
Create five separate binary logistic regression models, one for each priority level.
Create a linear regression model using model_type='LINEAR_REG' to predict priority as a numeric value from 0 to 4.
Create a k-means clustering model using model_type='KMEANS' with k=5 to group tickets.

explanation: A is correct because BigQuery ML's logistic regression automatically handles multiclass classification when the target variable has more than two categories, providing a single unified model. B is not correct because while this approach (one-vs-rest) works, it's unnecessarily complex and requires managing multiple models when a single multiclass model is more efficient and maintainable. C is not correct because linear regression treats the output as continuous numeric values, not discrete categories, which can produce invalid predictions like 2.7 that don't correspond to actual priority levels. D is not correct because k-means is unsupervised clustering and doesn't use the labeled data to learn the relationship between features and priority levels.

question_text: An e-commerce company wants to segment customers into distinct groups based on their browsing behavior, purchase history, and demographic information for targeted marketing campaigns. They have no predefined categories. Which BigQuery ML approach should you use?

options.text: Create a k-means clustering model using model_type='KMEANS' to discover natural customer segments without predefined labels.
Create a logistic regression model using model_type='LOGISTIC_REG' to classify customers into segments.
Create a boosted tree classifier using model_type='BOOSTED_TREE_CLASSIFIER' to categorize customers.
Create a matrix factorization model using model_type='MATRIX_FACTORIZATION' to group similar customers.

explanation: A is correct because k-means clustering is an unsupervised learning algorithm ideal for discovering natural groupings in data when no predefined categories exist. B is not correct because logistic regression is a supervised algorithm requiring labeled training data with predefined categories. C is not correct because boosted tree classifiers also require labeled data with known categories, which doesn't exist in this scenario. D is not correct because matrix factorization is designed for recommendation systems with user-item interactions, not for general customer segmentation based on features.

Create a boosted tree classifier using model_type='BOOSTED_TREE_CLASSIFIER' to categorize house values.
Create a k-means clustering model using model_type='KMEANS' to group houses by similar prices.

C is not correct because the classifier would categorize into price ranges rather than predict exact dollar amounts, losing precision. Create a matrix factorization model using model_type='MATRIX_FACTORIZATION' to predict usage patterns.

question_text: You are building a BigQuery ML model to predict customer churn, and you have 30 features including both categorical variables (e.g., product type, region) and numeric variables (e.g., account age, transaction count). You want to improve model performance by creating interaction features and polynomial features. How should you implement this in BigQuery ML?

options.text: Use the TRANSFORM clause in CREATE MODEL to define feature engineering operations like ML.POLYNOMIAL_EXPAND and ML.FEATURE_CROSS that will be applied consistently during training and prediction.
Create a separate preprocessing query that materializes the engineered features into a new table, then train the model on this table.
Use BigQuery SQL to create all engineered features in the training query SELECT statement before the CREATE MODEL statement.
Export the data to Vertex AI Workbench, use pandas to create the features, save back to BigQuery, then train the model.

explanation: A is correct because the TRANSFORM clause ensures that feature engineering is applied consistently during both training and prediction, preventing training-serving skew. ML.POLYNOMIAL_EXPAND and ML.FEATURE_CROSS are built-in functions for creating these features. B is not correct because materializing features into a separate table requires manually ensuring the same transformations are applied at prediction time, increasing the risk of inconsistency. C is not correct because feature engineering in the SELECT statement outside the model definition doesn't automatically apply those transformations during prediction. D is not correct because exporting data adds unnecessary complexity and latency, and doesn't leverage BigQuery ML's native feature engineering capabilities.

question_text: Your marketing team trained a BigQuery ML model that predicts customer purchase probability. The model uses 45 features, but you suspect many are not contributing to predictions. You want to identify and remove uninformative features to simplify the model while maintaining performance. What should you do?

options.text: Train a model with L1_REG parameter to encourage sparsity, then use ML.WEIGHTS to identify features with non-zero coefficients and retrain with only those features.
Use ML.FEATURE_INFO to get feature importance scores after training, manually calculate feature correlations, and remove features below a certain threshold.
Train a boosted tree model instead and use ML.GLOBAL_EXPLAIN to get feature importance, then select top features for a simpler model.
Create multiple models with different random subsets of features and select the subset that performs best on the validation set.

explanation: A is correct because L1 regularization (Lasso) automatically performs feature selection by driving uninformative feature coefficients to exactly zero, and ML.WEIGHTS provides a clear view of which features remain important. B is not correct because while ML.FEATURE_INFO provides insights, manually calculating correlations and setting thresholds is subjective and doesn't automatically optimize for the best feature subset. C is not correct because while boosted trees provide feature importance, this requires switching model types and doesn't directly simplify the original model architecture. D is not correct because random feature subset selection is inefficient compared to L1 regularization's principled approach to feature selection.

question_text: You have text data containing customer reviews that you want to use as features in a BigQuery ML sentiment classification model. The reviews are stored in a TEXT column. How should you prepare this text data for the model?

options.text: Use ML.NGRAMS in the TRANSFORM clause to automatically extract n-gram features from the text, which BigQuery ML will convert to TF-IDF representations.
Manually tokenize the text using BigQuery string functions like SPLIT, create a vocabulary table, and one-hot encode each word.
Export reviews to Cloud Storage, use the Natural Language API to get embeddings, import embeddings back to BigQuery, and use as features.
Use REGEXP_EXTRACT to extract specific keywords and phrases from the text, then use these as categorical features.

explanation: A is correct because ML.NGRAMS is BigQuery ML's built-in function for text feature extraction that automatically handles tokenization and TF-IDF transformation, making it the most efficient native solution. B is not correct because manual tokenization and one-hot encoding is complex, inefficient for high-cardinality vocabulary, and doesn't leverage BigQuery ML's optimized text processing. C is not correct because using an external API adds latency, cost, and complexity when BigQuery ML has native text handling capabilities. D is not correct because manually extracting keywords requires domain knowledge, is not scalable, and misses the semantic information that n-grams and TF-IDF capture automatically.

question_text: Your BigQuery ML model uses customer age as a feature, but you've noticed that the model performs poorly for customers in certain age ranges. You want to create age buckets (e.g., 18-25, 26-35, 36-50, 51+) to help the model better capture non-linear relationships. What's the best approach?

options.text: Use ML.BUCKETIZE in the TRANSFORM clause to automatically create quantile-based age buckets that will be consistently applied during training and prediction.
Create age buckets using CASE statements in the training query and manually apply the same logic in prediction queries.
Create a separate lookup table mapping age values to buckets and JOIN this table during both training and prediction.
Use ML.POLYNOMIAL_EXPAND to create polynomial features of age, which will capture non-linear effects.

explanation: A is correct because ML.BUCKETIZE in the TRANSFORM clause automatically creates consistent buckets and ensures they're applied identically during prediction, preventing training-serving skew. B is not correct because manually applying CASE statements in separate queries is error-prone and requires maintaining the same logic in multiple places. C is not correct because using a lookup table adds complexity and requires managing a separate table, plus it doesn't guarantee the exact same bucketing strategy at prediction time. D is not correct because while polynomial features capture non-linearity, they don't create discrete buckets as requested and may not capture the specific age-range effects as effectively as explicit bucketing.

question_text: You're building a BigQuery ML model with features that have very different scales: income ranges from $0 to $500,000, age from 18 to 100, and transaction counts from 0 to 10. You're concerned about feature scale affecting model training. What should you do?

options.text: Use ML.STANDARD_SCALER or ML.MIN_MAX_SCALER in the TRANSFORM clause to normalize features, which BigQuery ML will apply consistently during training and prediction.
Don't worry about scaling because BigQuery ML automatically handles feature normalization for all model types.
Manually calculate mean and standard deviation for each feature, then apply z-score normalization in SQL before training.
Use log transformation on all features to bring them to similar scales before training the model.

explanation: A is correct because ML.STANDARD_SCALER (z-score normalization) and ML.MIN_MAX_SCALER in the TRANSFORM clause provide consistent, automatic feature scaling during both training and prediction, which is crucial for distance-based algorithms. B is not correct because BigQuery ML does not automatically normalize features for all model types; some models like linear regression benefit from explicit normalization. C is not correct because manually calculating normalization parameters and applying them doesn't guarantee consistency at prediction time and increases maintenance burden. D is not correct because log transformation changes the distribution and isn't appropriate for all features (especially those with zeros or negative values), and doesn't guarantee features are on similar scales.

question_text: Your BigQuery dataset has a 'region' categorical feature with 50 different values. You want to use this feature in a BigQuery ML model, but you're concerned about the high cardinality. How should you handle this feature?

options.text: Use the region feature directly in BigQuery ML, which will automatically one-hot encode categorical variables during training.
Manually create 50 binary columns (one for each region) using CASE statements before training the model.
Use ML.BUCKETIZE to reduce the number of regions into fewer groups based on some business logic.
Convert region names to numeric IDs (1-50) and use as a single numeric feature.

explanation: A is correct because BigQuery ML automatically handles categorical features by applying one-hot encoding, making it the simplest and most maintainable approach. B is not correct because manually creating binary columns is tedious, error-prone, and doesn't automatically apply at prediction time, defeating the purpose of BigQuery ML's automatic handling. C is not correct because ML.BUCKETIZE is for continuous variables, not categorical ones, and arbitrarily grouping regions loses information. D is not correct because converting categorical values to numeric IDs imposes an artificial ordinal relationship that doesn't exist (region 1 is not 'less than' region 2), which can mislead the model.

question_text: You trained a BigQuery ML model, and you want to understand which features are most important in making predictions. You need to generate feature importance scores. What should you do?

options.text: For tree-based models, use ML.GLOBAL_EXPLAIN to get feature importance scores based on information gain. For linear models, use ML.WEIGHTS to examine coefficient magnitudes.
Use ML.FEATURE_INFO which provides feature importance for all model types in BigQuery ML.
Export the model to Vertex AI and use Vertex Explainable AI to generate feature importance scores.
Retrain the model multiple times, removing one feature at a time, and measure the impact on model performance.

question_text: Your dataset has a date column that you want to use for prediction. You believe day of week and month might be important predictors. How should you engineer these features in BigQuery ML?

options.text: Use ML.EXTRACT_DAY_OF_WEEK and ML.EXTRACT_MONTH in the TRANSFORM clause to extract temporal components that will be automatically applied during prediction.
Use standard BigQuery date functions like EXTRACT(DAYOFWEEK FROM date) and EXTRACT(MONTH FROM date) in the TRANSFORM clause.
Create separate columns for day of week and month using EXTRACT functions in a preprocessing query, then train on the preprocessed table.
Use the date column directly and let BigQuery ML automatically extract relevant temporal features.

A is not correct because ML.EXTRACT_DAY_OF_WEEK and ML.EXTRACT_MONTH are not actual BigQuery ML functions; the correct approach uses standard EXTRACT. C is not correct because preprocessing in a separate query doesn't automatically apply transformations at prediction time, risking training-serving skew. question_text: You have a trained BigQuery ML model for customer churn prediction. Now you need to generate predictions for all active customers and store the results in a new BigQuery table for the marketing team to use. What's the most efficient approach?

options.text: Use ML.PREDICT with a CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE statement to generate predictions and store them in a new table in a single query.
Use ML.PREDICT to generate predictions, export results to Cloud Storage as CSV, then import back to BigQuery as a new table.
Write a Python script that queries BigQuery for customer data, calls ML.PREDICT for each customer individually, and inserts results into a new table.
Use the BigQuery API to export the model, run predictions in Vertex AI, then import predictions back to BigQuery.

explanation: A is correct because ML.PREDICT combined with CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE performs batch prediction efficiently within BigQuery, generating and storing all predictions in a single operation without data movement. B is not correct because exporting to Cloud Storage and reimporting adds unnecessary steps, latency, and complexity when predictions can be generated and stored directly in BigQuery. C is not correct because row-by-row prediction is extremely inefficient compared to batch prediction and unnecessarily complicates the process. D is not correct because moving the model to Vertex AI adds significant complexity and data transfer overhead when BigQuery ML can perform predictions natively.

Use scheduled queries in BigQuery to pre-compute predictions for all possible transaction patterns and cache results in Memorystore.
Keep the model in BigQuery and configure BigQuery BI Engine to cache prediction results for low latency.

question_text: You need to generate probability scores for each class in a multiclass classification model rather than just the predicted class. Your BigQuery ML model predicts customer segment (A, B, C, D). How do you get the probability distribution?

Add an option RETURN_PROBABILITIES=TRUE to the ML.PREDICT function call.
Use ML.EVALUATE to get probability scores for each class on the prediction dataset.

options.text: Include promotional campaign data as covariates (additional features) in the ARIMA_PLUS model training, then provide future promotion values in the ML.FORECAST query using the HORIZON and future covariate values.
Train separate ARIMA_PLUS models for periods with and without promotions, then manually combine their forecasts based on the promotional calendar.

question_text: You have a dataset for training AutoML Tables with 100,000 rows. AutoML requires splitting data into training, validation, and test sets. How should you handle this?

options.text: Let AutoML automatically split the data using random sampling, or manually specify a split column if you need control over which data goes into each set.
Manually create three separate CSV files for training, validation, and test sets before uploading.
Upload all data as training data; AutoML doesn't use validation or test sets.
Use BigQuery to randomly split the data into three tables, then import each separately.

explanation: A is correct because AutoML Tables can automatically handle data splitting with proper random sampling, or you can specify a manual split column for more control (useful for time-series or when you want specific data in test sets). B is not correct because AutoML can handle splitting automatically, making manual file creation unnecessary. C is not correct because AutoML uses validation data for model selection and test data for final evaluation; these splits are essential. D is not correct because while this works, it's more complex than necessary when AutoML provides built-in splitting functionality.

source.pdf_name: Professional Machine Learning Engineer Sample Questions.pdf

question_text: Your company wants to classify support tickets into urgent and non-urgent categories using AutoML Natural Language. You have 5,000 labeled tickets, but 95% are non-urgent. What should you do before training?

options.text: Address the class imbalance by either collecting more urgent ticket examples or using AutoML's class weight balancing option to ensure the model learns both classes effectively.
Train the model as-is; AutoML will automatically detect and handle imbalanced classes.
Randomly duplicate urgent tickets until both classes have equal representation.
Remove non-urgent tickets until the dataset is balanced at 50/50.

explanation: A is correct because severe class imbalance can lead to models that ignore the minority class, so addressing it through more data collection or class balancing options improves model quality. B is not correct because while AutoML handles some imbalance, 95/5 split is severe and benefits from explicit intervention. C is not correct because simple duplication can lead to overfitting on the minority class and doesn't add new information. D is not correct because removing 90% of your data wastes valuable training examples and may not leave enough data for effective training.

source.pdf_name: Professional Machine Learning Engineer Sample Questions.pdf

question_text: You're building an AutoML Vision model to detect manufacturing defects in products. Your training images are high-resolution (4000x3000 pixels) and defects are small (50x50 pixels). How should you prepare the images?

options.text: Keep the high-resolution images as AutoML Vision can handle them and will preserve the detail needed to detect small defects during preprocessing.
Resize all images to 224x224 pixels to match standard computer vision model input sizes.
Crop each image to just the defect region to make the defects more prominent.
Convert images to grayscale to reduce file size and speed up training.

explanation: A is correct because AutoML Vision handles high-resolution images and preserves necessary detail during its preprocessing, which is crucial for detecting small defects. B is not correct because aggressive downsampling would lose the detail needed to identify small defects, and AutoML handles image sizing appropriately. C is not correct because cropping removes context that may be important for defect detection and changes the problem from detection to classification. D is not correct because color information may be important for defect identification, and AutoML handles file size efficiently.

source.pdf_name: Professional Machine Learning Engineer Sample Questions.pdf

question_text: You trained an AutoML Tables model to predict customer lifetime value, and the model shows good overall metrics but performs poorly on high-value customers (top 5%). You need to improve predictions for this segment. What should you do?

options.text: Collect more training examples of high-value customers, or use optimization objectives in AutoML that focus on reducing error for high-value predictions rather than average error.
Train a separate AutoML model specifically for high-value customers using only those examples.
Remove high-value customers from training data as outliers and handle them with business rules.
Cap all customer lifetime values at the 95th percentile before training.

explanation: A is correct because adding more examples of the underrepresented segment and using appropriate optimization objectives helps the model learn patterns for high-value customers. B is not correct because splitting into separate models loses the benefit of learning from the full distribution and requires managing multiple models. C is not correct because high-value customers are exactly what you want to predict well, not exclude from the model. D is not correct because capping values prevents the model from learning to predict actual high values, defeating the purpose.

source.pdf_name: Professional Machine Learning Engineer Sample Questions.pdf

question_text: You're using AutoML Video to classify video content into categories. Your videos vary in length from 10 seconds to 10 minutes. How should you prepare the videos for training?

options.text: Upload videos with varying lengths directly to AutoML Video, which can handle different video durations and will sample frames appropriately for training.
Split all videos into uniform 30-second clips before uploading.
Extract key frames from each video and train an AutoML Vision image classification model instead.
Pad short videos with black frames to match the longest video duration.

explanation: A is correct because AutoML Video is designed to handle videos of varying lengths and automatically samples and processes them appropriately for training. B is not correct because splitting videos can break important temporal context and create artificial segments that don't represent natural video content. C is not correct because converting to image classification loses the temporal and motion information that video classification models leverage. D is not correct because padding with black frames adds no information and wastes computational resources.

source.pdf_name: Professional Machine Learning Engineer Sample Questions.pdf

question_text: Your AutoML Natural Language text classification model needs to categorize customer emails. Some emails are very short (one sentence) while others are long (multiple paragraphs). Does this affect training?

options.text: No, AutoML Natural Language can handle variable text lengths automatically. The model will process short and long texts appropriately without requiring uniform length.
Yes, truncate all emails to exactly 100 words to ensure uniform input size.
Yes, pad short emails with filler text to match the length of long emails.
Yes, train separate models for short emails and long emails.

explanation: A is correct because AutoML Natural Language is built on transformer-based architectures that naturally handle variable-length text through attention mechanisms. B is not correct because truncation loses information from longer emails and is unnecessary since the model handles length variation. C is not correct because padding with filler text adds noise and doesn't improve model performance. D is not correct because splitting into separate models adds complexity without benefit when a single model can handle both.

source.pdf_name: Professional Machine Learning Engineer Sample Questions.pdf

question_text: You're training an AutoML Tables model and notice that one feature, 'customer_id', has a perfect correlation with the target variable in your training data but shouldn't be predictive in production. What should you do?

options.text: Exclude customer_id from the model features, as it represents data leakage - the model is learning an identifier rather than generalizable patterns.
Keep customer_id since AutoML will automatically determine if it's useful.
Use customer_id in training but remove it during inference.
Hash customer_id values to make them more generic before training.

explanation: A is correct because customer_id represents data leakage - it's a unique identifier that doesn't provide generalizable predictive power and will cause the model to fail on new customers. B is not correct because AutoML may use any provided feature that appears predictive in training, even if it represents leakage. C is not correct because training with customer_id means the model learns to rely on it, and removing it at inference breaks the model's learned patterns. D is not correct because hashing still maintains the unique identifier problem; the model will learn to associate specific hash values with outcomes.

source.pdf_name: Professional Machine Learning Engineer Sample Questions.pdf

question_text: You trained an AutoML Vision model for image classification, and it achieved 95% accuracy on the validation set. However, when you test it on recent images from production, accuracy drops to 75%. What's the most likely cause?

options.text: Training-serving skew due to distribution shift - the production images have different characteristics (lighting, angles, quality) than the training data. Collect recent production images and retrain.
The model is overfitting and needs more regularization during training.
AutoML Vision models naturally degrade over time and need to be retrained monthly.
The production images are too large and need to be resized to match training image sizes.

explanation: A is correct because the significant accuracy drop on production data suggests distribution shift - the production images differ from training data in ways the model hasn't learned. Including recent production data in training addresses this. B is not correct because overfitting would show poor validation accuracy, not a gap between validation and production performance. C is not correct because models don't naturally degrade over time unless the data distribution changes. D is not correct because AutoML handles image sizing automatically during inference, so size alone wouldn't cause this accuracy drop.

source.pdf_name: Professional Machine Learning Engineer Sample Questions.pdf

question_text: Your AutoML Tables model training failed with an error message about insufficient data. You have 1,000 rows and 50 features. What's the most likely issue?

options.text: The target variable has too few examples per class. Check that each class has at least 50-100 examples and the dataset meets AutoML's minimum data requirements.
The dataset is too small overall; AutoML Tables requires at least 10,000 rows.
There are too many features (50) for the number of rows (1,000).
The CSV file format is incorrect and needs to be converted to JSON.

explanation: A is correct because AutoML requires sufficient examples per class for reliable training, and with 1,000 rows, if you have many classes, some may have too few examples. B is not correct because AutoML Tables can work with as few as 1,000 rows total, though more is better. C is not correct because 1,000 rows with 50 features is a reasonable ratio for AutoML, which handles high-dimensional data well. D is not correct because AutoML Tables accepts CSV format, and format errors would produce different error messages.

source.pdf_name: Professional Machine Learning Engineer Sample Questions.pdf

question_text: You're using AutoML Forecasting to predict daily product demand for the next 30 days. You have 2 years of historical daily sales data. The data shows strong weekly seasonality (weekends vs weekdays) and yearly seasonality (holidays). How should you configure the model?

options.text: Enable both weekly and yearly seasonality patterns in AutoML Forecasting, and include holiday information as additional time-series covariates for better predictions.
AutoML Forecasting automatically detects all seasonality patterns; no configuration needed.
Use only yearly seasonality since it's more important than weekly patterns.
Pre-process the data to remove seasonality before training, then add it back to predictions.

explanation: A is correct because AutoML Forecasting allows you to specify multiple seasonality patterns and covariates, which improves forecast accuracy when these patterns exist in your data. B is not correct because while AutoML can detect some patterns automatically, explicitly configuring known seasonality and providing holiday information improves model performance. C is not correct because ignoring weekly seasonality loses important predictive information, especially for daily forecasts. D is not correct because manually removing and re-adding seasonality is complex and error-prone when AutoML can model seasonality directly.

source.pdf_name: Professional Machine Learning Engineer Sample Questions.pdf

question_text: Your AutoML Forecasting model needs to predict sales for 100 different stores. Each store has unique characteristics. How should you structure your training data?

options.text: Include all stores in a single dataset with a 'store_id' column configured as the time series identifier, allowing AutoML to train one model that learns patterns across all stores.
Train 100 separate AutoML Forecasting models, one for each store.
Aggregate all store sales into a single time series and forecast the total.
Randomly sample 10 representative stores and train a model on those only.

explanation: A is correct because AutoML Forecasting supports multiple time series through a time series identifier column, enabling the model to learn from patterns across all stores while making store-specific predictions. B is not correct because managing 100 separate models is operationally complex and loses the benefit of learning shared patterns across stores. C is not correct because aggregating loses store-specific patterns and makes individual store forecasts impossible. D is not correct because sampling loses data from 90 stores and prevents forecasting for stores not in the sample.

source.pdf_name: Professional Machine Learning Engineer Sample Questions.pdf

question_text: You trained an AutoML Natural Language sentiment classification model, and it performs well overall but consistently misclassifies sarcastic reviews as positive. What should you do?

options.text: Add more labeled examples of sarcastic reviews to the training data so the model can learn to recognize sarcasm patterns and linguistic cues.
Use a different AutoML optimization objective focused on precision rather than accuracy.
Pre-process text to detect and remove sarcasm before feeding to the model.
AutoML Natural Language cannot learn sarcasm; switch to a custom TensorFlow model.

explanation: A is correct because the model needs more training examples of sarcasm to learn its linguistic patterns and contextual cues. B is not correct because changing the optimization objective doesn't help the model learn to identify sarcasm; it only changes how errors are weighted. C is not correct because detecting sarcasm is itself a complex NLP task, and removing it loses information rather than improving classification. D is not correct because AutoML Natural Language uses sophisticated language models that can learn sarcasm patterns if given sufficient training examples.

source.pdf_name: Professional Machine Learning Engineer Sample Questions.pdf

question_text: Your AutoML Forecasting model shows good historical fit but poor forecast accuracy for the next 30 days. You suspect that recent market changes aren't captured in historical data. What should you do?

options.text: Add recent external factors as time-series covariates (e.g., economic indicators, marketing campaigns, competitor activity) to help the model account for changing market conditions.
Increase the forecast horizon from 30 days to 90 days to give the model more data.
Remove the oldest historical data and train only on the most recent 3 months.
Switch from AutoML Forecasting to AutoML Tables for better accuracy.

explanation: A is correct because covariates allow the model to incorporate external factors that influence forecasts but aren't captured in historical patterns alone. B is not correct because increasing the forecast horizon doesn't address the market change issue; it makes predictions even harder. C is not correct because using only recent data loses historical patterns and seasonality information, and may not be enough data for reliable training. D is not correct because AutoML Tables isn't designed for time-series forecasting; the issue is missing information, not the wrong model type.

source.pdf_name: Professional Machine Learning Engineer Sample Questions.pdf

question_text: You're using AutoML Vision for object detection, and the model performs poorly on small objects but well on large objects. The training data has equal numbers of small and large objects. What should you do?

options.text: Increase training time or budget to allow AutoML to explore more model architectures that better handle multi-scale objects, and verify that bounding boxes for small objects are accurately labeled.
Remove all large objects from training data to force the model to focus on small objects.
Crop images to only show small objects before training.
Train two separate models - one for small objects and one for large objects.

explanation: A is correct because more training time allows AutoML to find better architectures for multi-scale detection, and accurate labeling is critical for small objects. B is not correct because removing large objects loses valuable training data and doesn't address the small object detection problem. C is not correct because cropping removes context and changes the problem from detection to classification. D is not correct because separate models add operational complexity and may miss objects of intermediate size.

source.pdf_name: Professional Machine Learning Engineer Sample Questions.pdf

question_text: Your AutoML Tables model training is taking much longer than expected. You have 500,000 rows and 200 features, with many high-cardinality categorical variables. What can you do to reduce training time?

options.text: Reduce the training budget in AutoML settings to limit the number of model trials and architecture searches, or remove features that have low predictive importance.
Delete 80% of the rows randomly to speed up training.
Convert all categorical variables to numeric codes before training.
Split the dataset into 10 smaller datasets and train 10 separate models.

explanation: A is correct because reducing the training budget limits the search space while still producing good models, and removing low-importance features reduces computational cost without much impact on accuracy. B is not correct because randomly deleting 80% of data significantly reduces model quality and loses valuable training information. C is not correct because AutoML already handles categorical encoding optimally; manual conversion doesn't reduce training time and may hurt performance. D is not correct because splitting data reduces the information available to each model and creates operational complexity.

source.pdf_name: Professional Machine Learning Engineer Sample Questions.pdf

question_text: You trained an AutoML Vision image classification model with 10 classes. The confusion matrix shows that two visually similar classes (Class A and Class B) are frequently confused with each other. What should you do?

options.text: Add more training examples for Classes A and B that highlight their distinguishing features, or consider merging them into a single class if the distinction isn't important for your use case.
Remove one of the classes entirely from the training data.
Train separate binary classifiers for each class pair to improve discrimination.
Apply stronger data augmentation to Classes A and B only.

explanation: A is correct because more training examples showing distinguishing features helps the model learn to separate similar classes, or merging avoids the confusion if the distinction isn't business-critical. B is not correct because removing a class doesn't solve the confusion problem and loses the ability to identify that class. C is not correct because managing multiple binary classifiers is complex and doesn't leverage AutoML's multi-class learning. D is not correct because augmentation alone doesn't add new information about distinguishing features; you need examples that highlight the actual differences.

source.pdf_name: Professional Machine Learning Engineer Sample Questions.pdf

question_text: Your AutoML Forecasting model for daily sales shows a large spike in forecast error during a recent holiday period that wasn't in the training data. How should you improve future forecasts during holidays?

options.text: Create a holiday calendar as a time-series covariate and include it in your forecasting model, marking known holidays for both historical and future periods.
Manually adjust forecasts by a fixed percentage during holiday periods.
Train a separate model using only data from holiday periods.
Remove holiday periods from training data as outliers.

explanation: A is correct because holiday covariates allow the model to learn holiday effects from historical data and apply them to future holiday forecasts systematically. B is not correct because manual adjustments don't leverage historical holiday patterns and require ongoing human intervention. C is not correct because holiday periods alone don't provide enough data for a reliable model, and you need a model that works for both holiday and non-holiday periods. D is not correct because holidays are real events that affect sales; removing them means the model won't learn to handle them.

source.pdf_name: Professional Machine Learning Engineer Sample Questions.pdf

question_text: You completed training an AutoML Tables model with a 3-hour training budget. The final model performance is good but not meeting your target accuracy. The feature importance shows one key feature wasn't used effectively. What should you do?

options.text: Increase the training budget to allow AutoML more time to explore different model architectures and feature combinations, or engineer additional features that might complement the underutilized key feature.
Manually increase the weight of that feature in the dataset by duplicating its values.
Remove all other features to force the model to focus on the key feature.
Accept the current performance; AutoML has found the optimal model already.

explanation: A is correct because increasing training budget allows AutoML to explore more model types and hyperparameters that might better utilize the key feature, and feature engineering can make the feature more useful. B is not correct because duplicating feature values doesn't change the underlying information and may confuse the model. C is not correct because removing other features loses valuable information; the goal is to better use all features together. D is not correct because if you haven't met your target and training was time-limited, additional search may find better models.

source.pdf_name: Professional Machine Learning Engineer Sample Questions.pdf

question_text: Your ML project requires organizing training data that includes customer demographics in CSV files, product images in JPEG format, and transaction logs in JSON files. All data is currently stored in separate Cloud Storage buckets. What's the best way to organize this data for model training?

options.text: Create a structured directory hierarchy in a single Cloud Storage bucket with separate folders for each data type (csv/, images/, json/) and use a manifest file to track data relationships.
Keep data in separate buckets and create symbolic links between related files.
Convert all data types to a single format (CSV) and store in one bucket.
Load all data into BigQuery tables with different schemas for each data type.

explanation: A is correct because a structured directory hierarchy with a manifest file provides clear organization, easy access patterns, and maintains relationships between different data types while preserving their native formats. B is not correct because Cloud Storage doesn't support symbolic links, and managing relationships across buckets adds complexity. C is not correct because converting images to CSV loses information and is impractical; each data type should maintain its optimal format. D is not correct because BigQuery isn't designed for storing binary data like images, and forcing all data into tables is inefficient.

source.pdf_name: Professional Machine Learning Engineer Sample Questions.pdf

question_text: You have 100,000 video files for a video classification project stored in Cloud Storage. Each video is 30 seconds to 5 minutes long. You need to prepare this data for training with Vertex AI. What should you do?

options.text: Keep videos in Cloud Storage with a standardized naming convention, create a CSV file with video paths and labels, and import this CSV into Vertex AI for training.
Extract individual frames from each video, save as images, and train an image classification model instead.
Transcode all videos to a uniform 1-minute length by trimming or padding.
Split videos into 10-second segments and treat each segment as a separate training example.

explanation: A is correct because Vertex AI can directly work with videos stored in Cloud Storage using a CSV manifest file, allowing videos of varying lengths without preprocessing. B is not correct because extracting frames loses temporal information crucial for video classification and creates a different problem. C is not correct because forcing uniform length through trimming or padding loses information or adds noise without improving model training. D is not correct because arbitrary segmentation breaks the natural video structure and doesn't match the actual classification task.

source.pdf_name: Professional Machine Learning Engineer Sample Questions.pdf

question_text: Your text classification project has training data consisting of 50,000 customer reviews stored as individual text files in Cloud Storage. You need to organize this data efficiently for model training. What should you do?

options.text: Create a CSV file where each row contains the Cloud Storage path to the text file and its label, then use this CSV as your training dataset.
Combine all text files into a single large text file with labels embedded between reviews.
Load all reviews into a BigQuery table with text content and labels as columns.
Convert each text file to a JSON object and store in Firestore for easy retrieval.

explanation: A is correct because a CSV manifest linking to individual files maintains data organization, allows easy updates, and works efficiently with Vertex AI's training pipelines. B is not correct because a single large file is harder to manage, doesn't allow parallel processing efficiently, and makes updates difficult. C is not correct because while BigQuery works for text data, it's unnecessary overhead when Cloud Storage with a CSV manifest is simpler and more cost-effective for this use case. D is not correct because Firestore is designed for operational data access, not ML training datasets, and adds unnecessary complexity and cost.

source.pdf_name: Professional Machine Learning Engineer Sample Questions.pdf

question_text: You're preparing image data for an object detection model. Your dataset includes 20,000 images with bounding box annotations stored in separate XML files (one per image). How should you organize this data?

options.text: Convert the XML annotations to CSV format with one row per bounding box, including image path, coordinates, and class labels, which is the standard format for Vertex AI object detection.
Keep XML files alongside images with matching filenames and let the training framework parse them automatically.
Embed annotation metadata directly into image EXIF data for unified storage.
Store annotations in a separate BigQuery table and join at training time.

explanation: A is correct because CSV format with bounding box coordinates is the standard input format for Vertex AI object detection, making the data ready for training. B is not correct because Vertex AI doesn't automatically parse XML annotations; you need to provide data in the expected CSV format. C is not correct because EXIF data has size limitations, doesn't support complex structures like multiple bounding boxes, and requires custom parsing. D is not correct because BigQuery adds unnecessary complexity for image annotations when a CSV file provides a simpler, more portable solution.

source.pdf_name: Professional Machine Learning Engineer Sample Questions.pdf

question_text: Your team has tabular training data with 100 features and 1 million rows currently stored in a PostgreSQL database. You need to prepare this data for training in Vertex AI. What's the most efficient approach?

options.text: Export the data from PostgreSQL to BigQuery, perform any necessary preprocessing in BigQuery, then train directly from BigQuery or export to Cloud Storage as needed.
Export to CSV files in Cloud Storage and train directly from the CSV files.
Keep data in PostgreSQL and query it directly during training using a custom data loader.
Export to Datastore for better integration with Google Cloud services.

explanation: A is correct because BigQuery provides efficient storage for large tabular datasets, powerful preprocessing capabilities with SQL, and native integration with Vertex AI for training. B is not correct because while CSV files work, BigQuery offers better performance for large datasets, easier preprocessing, and native Vertex AI integration. C is not correct because querying PostgreSQL during training adds latency, isn't cost-effective, and creates dependencies on the operational database. D is not correct because Datastore is designed for NoSQL operational workloads, not large-scale analytical ML training datasets.

source.pdf_name: Professional Machine Learning Engineer Sample Questions.pdf

question_text: You have audio recordings for a speech recognition project. The recordings are in various formats (WAV, MP3, FLAC) and different sample rates (16kHz, 44.1kHz, 48kHz). How should you organize this data?

options.text: Store original files in Cloud Storage, create a CSV manifest with file paths and metadata (format, sample rate, duration), and let the training pipeline handle format conversion as needed.
Convert all audio to a single format (WAV at 16kHz) before storing in Cloud Storage.
Store only the highest quality versions and discard lower quality recordings.
Organize files into separate buckets based on format and sample rate.

explanation: A is correct because preserving original formats maintains data fidelity while the manifest provides necessary metadata, and modern training pipelines can handle format conversion on-the-fly. B is not correct because pre-converting all files is time-consuming, potentially degrades quality, and isn't necessary when training frameworks can handle various formats. C is not correct because different quality levels may represent real-world variations important for model robustness. D is not correct because separating into multiple buckets based on format creates unnecessary complexity when a single bucket with good naming and a manifest is simpler.

source.pdf_name: Professional Machine Learning Engineer Sample Questions.pdf

question_text: Your ML project needs to combine data from multiple sources: sensor data streamed to Pub/Sub, historical records in BigQuery, and configuration files in Cloud Storage. How should you organize this data for exploration and model development?

options.text: Use Dataflow to process streaming data and join it with BigQuery historical data, then write unified results to BigQuery for exploration, keeping configuration files referenced from Cloud Storage.
Store all data types in Cloud Storage as JSON files for uniform access.
Create separate processing pipelines for each data source and combine results at model training time.
Load everything into a single Bigtable instance for unified access.

explanation: A is correct because Dataflow provides stream processing capabilities, BigQuery offers efficient storage and querying for combined data, and Cloud Storage is appropriate for configuration files, creating a cohesive data pipeline. B is not correct because converting structured data and streams to JSON files loses BigQuery's query capabilities and doesn't handle streaming data efficiently. C is not correct because separate pipelines without integration makes data exploration and feature engineering harder. D is not correct because Bigtable is designed for high-throughput operational workloads, not analytical ML data exploration and joining.

source.pdf_name: Professional Machine Learning Engineer Sample Questions.pdf

question_text: You need to version control your training datasets which include both tabular data in BigQuery and image files in Cloud Storage. The data changes monthly as new data is added. How should you manage dataset versions?

options.text: Use BigQuery table snapshots for tabular data and Cloud Storage object versioning with dated folder prefixes for images, maintaining a manifest file that references specific versions.
Create new BigQuery datasets and Storage buckets for each version with version numbers in names.
Use Git LFS to version control all data including images and BigQuery exports.
Keep only the latest version and document changes in a separate spreadsheet.

explanation: A is correct because BigQuery snapshots provide efficient versioning for tabular data, Cloud Storage versioning maintains image history, and a manifest file tracks the specific versions used together. B is not correct because creating separate datasets and buckets for each version leads to storage bloat and management complexity. C is not correct because Git LFS isn't designed for large-scale ML datasets, especially multi-GB images and BigQuery tables. D is not correct because keeping only the latest version prevents reproducing previous model training runs and comparing results.

source.pdf_name: Professional Machine Learning Engineer Sample Questions.pdf

question_text: You have 5TB of training data in BigQuery that needs preprocessing including feature scaling, one-hot encoding, and missing value imputation. The preprocessing must be consistent between training and serving. You want to use the same preprocessing logic for both batch and online scenarios. What should you do?

options.text: Use TensorFlow Transform (TFX) to define preprocessing in a transform function that generates a preprocessing graph, which can be applied consistently during both training and serving.
Write preprocessing logic in BigQuery SQL and manually replicate the same logic in your serving code.
Preprocess data in BigQuery and save both raw and processed versions, using processed data for training and raw data for serving with separate preprocessing.
Use pandas in Vertex AI Workbench for preprocessing and document the steps for manual replication at serving time.

explanation: A is correct because TFX Transform creates a preprocessing graph that can be saved and applied identically during training and serving, preventing training-serving skew. B is not correct because manually replicating logic is error-prone and doesn't guarantee consistency, especially for operations like scaling that depend on training data statistics. C is not correct because using different preprocessing at serving time defeats the purpose and introduces training-serving skew. D is not correct because manual documentation doesn't ensure consistency and is prone to implementation differences between training and serving.

source.pdf_name: Professional Machine Learning Engineer Sample Questions.pdf

question_text: Your streaming ML pipeline receives real-time transaction data through Pub/Sub that needs to be preprocessed (windowing aggregations, feature extraction) before model inference. Processing must handle late-arriving data and out-of-order events. What should you do?

options.text: Use Dataflow with windowing operations to aggregate streaming data, allowing watermarks and triggers to handle late-arriving data, then perform feature extraction before sending to the model.
Use Cloud Functions triggered by Pub/Sub to process each message individually and maintain state in Memorystore.
Write messages to BigQuery first, then run scheduled queries every minute to aggregate and extract features.
Use a custom Python application on Compute Engine that subscribes to Pub/Sub and processes messages in-memory.

explanation: A is correct because Dataflow is designed for stream processing with built-in windowing, watermarks, and triggers that handle late data and out-of-order events correctly. B is not correct because Cloud Functions are stateless and don't natively handle windowing or late data; managing state in Memorystore adds complexity. C is not correct because scheduled queries don't provide true real-time processing and can't handle late-arriving data within the same window correctly. D is not correct because building custom stream processing doesn't leverage managed services and requires implementing complex windowing and late-data handling logic.

source.pdf_name: Professional Machine Learning Engineer Sample Questions.pdf

question_text: You need to preprocess 100 million images for training by resizing, normalizing pixel values, and applying data augmentation. The preprocessing should be done efficiently and be reproducible. What should you do?

options.text: Use TFX with a preprocessing component that applies TensorFlow data augmentation and transformations as part of the training pipeline, processing images on-the-fly during training.
Write a Dataflow job to preprocess all images and save preprocessed versions to Cloud Storage before training.
Use a Vertex AI Workbench notebook with PIL/OpenCV to preprocess images locally and upload results.
Use Cloud Functions to preprocess each image when uploaded to Cloud Storage.

explanation: A is correct because TFX enables on-the-fly preprocessing as part of the training pipeline, avoiding storage of intermediate preprocessed images and allowing different augmentations per epoch. B is not correct because preprocessing 100M images and storing results doubles storage costs and loses the benefit of per-epoch random augmentation. C is not correct because local preprocessing on a notebook doesn't scale to 100M images and isn't efficient. D is not correct because Cloud Functions have execution time limits and preprocessing on upload doesn't support training-time augmentation variations.

source.pdf_name: Professional Machine Learning Engineer Sample Questions.pdf

question_text: Your tabular dataset in BigQuery has 20% missing values across various features. You need to impute missing values using appropriate strategies (mean for numeric, mode for categorical) and ensure the same imputation is applied during serving. What should you do?

options.text: Use TensorFlow Transform to compute imputation statistics (mean, mode) from the training data and create a preprocessing graph that applies these statistics consistently during both training and serving.
Calculate imputation values in BigQuery, fill missing values, and document the values for manual application at serving time.
Use BigQuery ML's automatic missing value handling and don't worry about serving consistency.
Remove all rows with missing values to avoid imputation complexity.

explanation: A is correct because TensorFlow Transform computes statistics from training data once and packages them in a reusable graph, ensuring identical imputation at serving time. B is not correct because manual documentation doesn't guarantee consistency and is error-prone when applied in production code. C is not correct because BigQuery ML's handling is for training only; you still need to apply the same logic at serving time for consistency. D is not correct because removing 20% of data significantly reduces training data and may introduce bias.

source.pdf_name: Professional Machine Learning Engineer Sample Questions.pdf

question_text: You need to perform feature engineering on time-series data in BigQuery, creating rolling averages and lag features. The features will be used for both batch and online predictions. How should you implement this preprocessing?

options.text: Create BigQuery SQL functions for feature calculation, use them in training queries, then replicate the same SQL logic in your serving pipeline to compute features on-demand.
Use Dataflow to compute rolling features and store them in Vertex AI Feature Store for consistent access during both training and serving.
Compute all possible feature values ahead of time and store in BigQuery for lookup during training and serving.
Use TensorFlow Transform to compute rolling features within the model graph.

explanation: B is correct because Dataflow can efficiently compute time-series features and Vertex AI Feature Store provides a centralized, versioned store that serves features consistently for both batch and online use cases. A is not correct because replicating SQL logic doesn't guarantee consistency and computing rolling features on-demand for online serving can be slow. C is not correct because pre-computing all possible feature values for time-series data is impractical and doesn't handle new time points. D is not correct because TensorFlow Transform isn't designed for complex time-series operations like rolling windows that require historical data.

source.pdf_name: Professional Machine Learning Engineer Sample Questions.pdf

question_text: Your dataset contains free-text customer reviews that need to be tokenized and converted to embeddings. You want preprocessing to be consistent and efficient. The reviews are stored in BigQuery. What should you do?

options.text: Use TFX with TensorFlow Transform to define text preprocessing (tokenization, embedding lookup) that can be packaged with your model for consistent serving.
Preprocess text in BigQuery using SQL string functions and save embedded representations to a new table.
Use Cloud Natural Language API to process text during training and serving.
Write a custom preprocessing script in Python and run it separately for training and serving data.

explanation: A is correct because TFX Transform allows you to define text preprocessing as part of the model pipeline, ensuring the same tokenization and embedding logic is applied consistently during training and serving. B is not correct because BigQuery SQL string functions are limited for NLP preprocessing, and pre-computed embeddings don't allow for model updates. C is not correct because calling an external API adds latency and cost for every prediction, and doesn't ensure consistency with training preprocessing. D is not correct because separate scripts for training and serving risk inconsistencies and don't guarantee the same tokenization.

source.pdf_name: Professional Machine Learning Engineer Sample Questions.pdf

question_text: You need to join data from three BigQuery tables (user profiles, transaction history, product catalog) and create features for training. The joins are computationally expensive and you'll retrain weekly. What's the most efficient approach?

options.text: Create a materialized view in BigQuery that performs the joins and feature calculations, and refresh it on a schedule before training.
Perform the joins in every training SQL query, letting BigQuery optimize the execution.
Use Dataflow to read from all three tables, perform joins, and write results to Cloud Storage.
Export each table to Cloud Storage as CSV, use pandas to join them in a notebook, then import back to BigQuery.

explanation: A is correct because materialized views pre-compute and cache the expensive join results, allowing fast access during training while automatically refreshing on schedule. B is not correct because repeating expensive joins every training run wastes compute resources and time when the results don't change between training runs. C is not correct because Dataflow adds unnecessary complexity for joins that BigQuery handles natively, and doesn't provide the caching benefits of materialized views. D is not correct because exporting and reimporting data is inefficient and loses BigQuery's query optimization capabilities.

source.pdf_name: Professional Machine Learning Engineer Sample Questions.pdf

question_text: Your preprocessing pipeline needs to scale categorical features with high cardinality (100,000+ unique values) using embeddings. You want to ensure consistent embedding lookup during training and serving. What should you do?

options.text: Use TensorFlow Transform to create a vocabulary file for categorical values during preprocessing, then include embedding layers in your model that reference this vocabulary.
One-hot encode all categorical values and use PCA to reduce dimensionality.
Hash all categorical values to a fixed number of buckets and use those as features.
Store pre-computed embeddings in a BigQuery table and look them up during training and serving.

explanation: A is correct because TensorFlow Transform creates a consistent vocabulary file from training data, and embedding layers in TensorFlow can reference this vocabulary for consistent lookup during serving. B is not correct because one-hot encoding 100,000+ categories creates extremely high-dimensional sparse features that are inefficient, and PCA requires fitting that doesn't easily transfer to serving. C is not correct because hashing introduces collisions that can hurt model performance, and doesn't learn optimal representations like embeddings do. D is not correct because pre-computed embeddings can't adapt to new categorical values and don't allow the model to learn optimal embeddings during training.

source.pdf_name: Professional Machine Learning Engineer Sample Questions.pdf

question_text: You're preprocessing sensor data that arrives in mini-batches through Pub/Sub. The preprocessing requires computing statistics over a 5-minute sliding window and extracting frequency-domain features. What should you do?

options.text: Use Dataflow with sliding window transformations to aggregate data, compute statistics, and apply Fourier transforms for frequency features before outputting to the model.
Use Cloud Functions to buffer data in Memorystore and compute windows manually.
Write all data to Bigtable first, then use a separate service to read and compute windowed features.
Store raw data in BigQuery and compute features with scheduled queries every minute.

explanation: A is correct because Dataflow provides native sliding window operations and can apply custom transforms like FFT for frequency features in a scalable streaming pipeline. B is not correct because implementing sliding windows manually in Cloud Functions is complex and error-prone, and managing state in Memorystore adds operational overhead. C is not correct because this two-step approach adds latency and complexity when Dataflow can process streams directly. D is not correct because scheduled queries don't provide true real-time processing needed for streaming data with 5-minute windows.

source.pdf_name: Professional Machine Learning Engineer Sample Questions.pdf

question_text: Your preprocessing involves normalizing numeric features using min-max scaling based on training data statistics. You need to apply the same scaling parameters during serving. How should you manage the scaling parameters?

options.text: Use TensorFlow Transform to compute min/max values from training data and save them in the transform graph, which is then loaded and applied during serving automatically.
Calculate min/max in BigQuery, store them in a configuration file, and load the file manually in serving code.
Recompute min/max from the serving data each time for dynamic scaling.
Hard-code typical min/max values based on domain knowledge.

explanation: A is correct because TensorFlow Transform packages the computed statistics (min/max) with the preprocessing logic, ensuring automatic and consistent application during serving. B is not correct because manual loading of configuration files is error-prone and doesn't guarantee the same preprocessing logic is applied correctly. C is not correct because recomputing from serving data introduces training-serving skew as serving statistics differ from training statistics. D is not correct because hard-coded values won't match actual training data distribution and introduce significant skew.

source.pdf_name: Professional Machine Learning Engineer Sample Questions.pdf

question_text: You need to preprocess log files containing semi-structured text data (timestamps, severity levels, message text) stored in Cloud Storage. The preprocessing includes parsing, filtering, and feature extraction for anomaly detection. What should you do?

Load all logs into BigQuery first using raw text format, then use SQL to parse and extract features.
Write a Python script in Vertex AI Workbench to process logs locally and save results.
Use Cloud Functions triggered by Cloud Storage to process each log file individually.

B is not correct because loading unparsed logs to BigQuery first is inefficient, and SQL isn't ideal for complex log parsing compared to Dataflow's programming model. C is not correct because local processing in a notebook doesn't scale to large log volumes and isn't suitable for production pipelines. D is not correct because Cloud Functions have execution time limits and processing files individually is inefficient for large batch processing.

source.pdf_name: Professional Machine Learning Engineer Sample Questions.pdf

Write custom SQL queries in BigQuery to check for data quality issues manually.
Assume the data is clean and handle errors during model training.
Use pandas profiling in a notebook to inspect data quality interactively.

explanation: A is correct because TFDV provides automated data validation, anomaly detection, and schema monitoring that integrates with TFX pipelines for systematic quality checks. B is not correct because manual SQL queries don't scale, require constant maintenance, and don't provide automated anomaly detection. C is not correct because ignoring data quality leads to poor model performance and can cause training failures. D is not correct because interactive profiling doesn't automate quality checks in production pipelines and requires manual inspection.

Copy all images to a single folder and let Vertex AI auto-detect categories from filenames.
Upload images directly through the Vertex AI console one by one.
Convert all images to TFRecord format first, then import to Vertex AI.

C is not correct because manual upload through console is impractical for large datasets and doesn't scale. source.pdf_name: Professional Machine Learning Engineer Sample Questions.pdf

Export data from BigQuery to CSV daily and reimport to Vertex AI as a new managed dataset.

Copy BigQuery data to a Vertex AI Feature Store and train from there.

Create separate Vertex AI projects for each dataset version.

question_text: You're setting up data labeling for images in Vertex AI and need human annotators to label 50,000 unlabeled images for classification. You want to optimize cost and quality. What should you do?

Send all 50,000 images for human labeling without any pre-filtering or assistance.
Use a pre-trained Vision AI model to label everything automatically without human review.
Randomly sample 10% of images for labeling and ignore the rest.

C is not correct because fully automated labeling without human review can introduce errors, especially for domain-specific categories.
